questions.question: The most important modifiable risk factor for stroke is:
questions.explanation: Others: smoking, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, dyslipidaemia.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: A transient ischaemic attack (TIA) is characterised by:

options.A: Focal neurological deficit resolving completely within 24 hours (usually minutes)

questions.explanation: TIAs are a warning of impending stroke.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: The NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) is used to measure:
questions.explanation: Scores range 0–42; higher scores indicate more severe stroke.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: The Fugl-Meyer Assessment evaluates:

options.B: Motor recovery after stroke (upper and lower limb)

questions.explanation: Based on Twitchell and Brunnstrom stages; maximum motor score 100.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: In a stroke patient with suspected dysphagia, the first step before oral feeding is:

options.D: A swallow screening and speech-language therapy assessment

questions.explanation: Aspiration pneumonia is a major cause of death.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: A patient with a left homonymous hemianopia has lost the:

options.A: Right half of the visual field in both eyes
options.C: Left half of the visual field in both eyes

questions.explanation: Right occipital lobe or optic tract lesion.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Apraxia is an inability to perform purposeful movements despite:
questions.explanation: Usually due to a left parietal or frontal lesion.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Inability to recognise objects through touch despite intact sensation is called:
questions.explanation: Parietal lobe lesion.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Body-weight supported treadmill training in stroke patients is used to:

options.B: Practise repetitive stepping with partial unloading to improve gait

questions.explanation: Evidence shows benefits for walking speed in non-ambulatory patients.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Mirror therapy after stroke aims to:

options.B: Use visual feedback of the unaffected limb to facilitate motor recovery of the affected side

questions.explanation: Also used for phantom limb pain and CRPS.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Functional electrical stimulation (FES) of the common peroneal nerve during gait is used to:

options.B: Provide dorsiflexion during swing in foot drop after stroke

questions.explanation: Triggered by a heel switch.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Which management avoids shoulder pain in the hemiplegic arm?

options.B: Correct positioning, support and avoiding pulling on the arm
options.D: Passive stretching above 90° without lateral rotation

questions.explanation: Painful shoulder worsens function and mood.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Associated reactions in hemiplegia are:

options.A: Involuntary movements of the affected limbs during effort of other body parts, e.g. yawning or coughing

questions.explanation: They increase tone and are reduced by relaxation.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: A hemiplegic gait is characterised by:

options.C: Circumduction of the affected leg with extended knee and plantar flexed foot

questions.explanation: Hip hiking and reduced arm swing are common.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: The single intervention shown to reduce mortality and disability after stroke is:

options.A: Care in an organised stroke unit

questions.explanation: Multidisciplinary stroke care improves outcomes.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Post-traumatic amnesia (PTA) refers to the period after head injury when the patient:

options.C: Is unable to lay down continuous new memories

questions.explanation: Its duration is a predictor of outcome.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Epidural haematoma typically results from a tear of the:

options.B: Middle meningeal artery with a lucid interval

questions.explanation: CT shows a biconvex (lens-shaped) collection.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: A chronic subdural haematoma is typically caused by rupture of:

options.A: Bridging veins, often in elderly or alcoholic patients

questions.explanation: CT shows a crescent-shaped collection.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Diffuse axonal injury results from:

options.D: Rotational acceleration–deceleration forces causing widespread shearing of axons

questions.explanation: Common in high-speed road traffic accidents; CT may be normal.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: In a patient with traumatic brain injury and agitation (Rancho IV), the therapist should:

options.C: Provide a calm, low-stimulation environment with short, consistent sessions

questions.explanation: Avoid confrontation.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Serial casting for plantar flexor contracture in brain injury works by:

options.A: Applying a sustained low-load stretch to lengthen the soft tissue

questions.explanation: Casts are changed every 3–7 days.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: The ‘pull test’ in Parkinson's disease evaluates:
questions.explanation: The therapist pulls the patient backward at the shoulders; more than 1–2 steps indicates impaired postural reflexes.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Progressively smaller handwriting is called:
questions.explanation: A feature of bradykinesia in Parkinson's disease.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: The ‘on–off phenomenon’ in Parkinson's disease refers to:

options.D: Fluctuations between good mobility and severe immobility related to levodopa dose

questions.explanation: Physiotherapy should be timed during the ‘on’ period.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Deep brain stimulation for Parkinson's disease usually targets the:

options.A: Subthalamic nucleus or globus pallidus interna

questions.explanation: Used when medication produces motor complications.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: The most common course of multiple sclerosis at onset is:
questions.explanation: About 85% start relapsing–remitting.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: A frequent presenting feature of multiple sclerosis is:

options.D: Optic neuritis with painful loss of vision in one eye

questions.explanation: Also internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Spasticity in multiple sclerosis is managed with:

options.C: Stretching, positioning, cooling and drugs such as baclofen

questions.explanation: Cooling lowers conduction block-related symptoms.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Exercise advice for patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is:
questions.explanation: Overwork weakness must be avoided.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Disease-modifying treatment for Guillain–Barré syndrome includes:
questions.explanation: Supportive respiratory care is essential.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: In myasthenia gravis, muscle strength temporarily improves after:

options.A: An anticholinesterase such as edrophonium or neostigmine

questions.explanation: Ice-pack test over the eyelid also improves ptosis.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: In Duchenne muscular dystrophy, the principle of physiotherapy is to:

options.B: Maintain mobility, prevent contractures and care for respiratory function; avoid heavy eccentric exercise

questions.explanation: Submaximal activity and stretching, night splints, respiratory monitoring.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: A complete spinal cord injury at which level is the highest that still leaves the intrinsic hand muscles (and therefore full upper-limb function) intact?
questions.explanation: T1 supplies the intrinsic muscles of the hand, so a complete lesion at T1 or below spares upper-limb function; C8 lesions leave partial intrinsic hand function.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: A patient with a complete T12 lesion would be expected to walk with:

options.B: KAFOs or RGO with crutches (exercise ambulation)

questions.explanation: Complete L3 can walk with KAFOs for household distances.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: An upper motor neurone (reflex) neurogenic bladder following a high spinal cord injury is characterised by:

options.C: Small, spastic bladder with detrusor–sphincter dyssynergia

questions.explanation: Intermittent catheterisation is the preferred management.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: In spinal cord injury heterotopic ossification commonly occurs at the:

options.C: Hip, below the level of the lesion

questions.explanation: Early signs: warmth, swelling and reduced range of motion; raised alkaline phosphatase.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Which drug is commonly used to treat spasticity in spinal cord injury?
questions.explanation: Also tizanidine, dantrolene, botulinum toxin and intrathecal baclofen.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: A patient with SCI developing new pain, ascending sensory loss and increasing weakness months after injury should be suspected of having:
questions.explanation: Requires MRI and neurosurgical referral.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: In a complete C5 tetraplegic patient, which respiratory muscles are mainly working?

options.A: Diaphragm and accessory neck muscles (with paralysed intercostals and abdominals)

questions.explanation: Assisted cough with manual compression of the abdomen.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: An abdominal binder in tetraplegia is applied to:

options.D: Maintain blood pressure in upright positions and support the diaphragm

questions.explanation: Reduces orthostatic hypotension and improves vital capacity in sitting.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: A pressure-relieving cushion for a paraplegic patient should be chosen to:

options.C: Distribute pressure and reduce shear at the ischial tuberosities
options.D: Eliminate the need for pressure relief

questions.explanation: Skin checks are mandatory.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Neurodevelopmental treatment (Bobath) in cerebral palsy emphasises:

options.D: Inhibition of abnormal reflex patterns and facilitation of normal movement through key points of control

questions.explanation: Handling with attention to postural alignment.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Selective dorsal rhizotomy is performed to:

options.A: Reduce spasticity in selected children with spastic diplegia

questions.explanation: Selective division of dorsal rootlets (L2–S1); requires intensive physiotherapy afterward.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: In spastic cerebral palsy, hip surveillance with pelvic radiographs is performed to detect:

options.B: Migration percentage of the femoral head (subluxation)

questions.explanation: Migration >30% may need surgery.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: A child with cerebral palsy and dynamic equinus often benefits from:

options.B: AFOs with or without botulinum toxin and stretching

questions.explanation: Surgery for fixed contracture.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: The parachute (protective extension) reflex appears at about:
questions.explanation: Lateral propping appears at 6–7 months and persists throughout life.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: The Landau reflex is elicited by:

options.C: Holding the infant prone in horizontal suspension: head lifts and trunk extends

questions.explanation: Present from about 3 months to 2 years.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: In the symmetrical tonic neck reflex, extending the neck causes:

options.A: Flexion of the arms and extension of the legs
options.D: Extension of the arms and flexion of the legs

questions.explanation: Persistence affects crawling and sitting.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: A child who cannot sit independently by 9 months should be:
questions.explanation: Early intervention improves outcomes.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Most infants achieve good head control by:
questions.explanation: Pull-to-sit shows no head lag by 4 months.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: After repair of a peripheral nerve, a major objective of physiotherapy is to:

options.A: Maintain joint mobility, prevent contractures, and protect insensate skin while awaiting reinnervation

questions.explanation: Recovery is ~1 mm/day.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Sensory re-education after nerve repair uses:

options.D: Graded discrimination of textures and objects with and without vision

questions.explanation: Phase 1 protection; phase 2 localisation; phase 3 discrimination.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Which treatment is central in complex regional pain syndrome type I?

options.C: Early graded motor imagery, desensitisation and mobilisation

questions.explanation: Immobilisation worsens the condition.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Physiotherapy for Bell's palsy emphasises:

options.C: Facial massage, gentle mirror exercises and eye protection; avoid vigorous electrical stimulation early

questions.explanation: Eye care prevents corneal ulceration.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Inability to close the eye in Bell's palsy is due to paralysis of the:
questions.explanation: Bell's phenomenon is upward deviation of the eyeball when attempting closure.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Conservative treatment of mild carpal tunnel syndrome includes:

options.D: Night wrist splints in neutral, activity modification and nerve gliding exercises

questions.explanation: Steroid injection or release if refractory.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Cooling a nerve will cause conduction velocity to:
questions.explanation: Approximately 2 m/s per degree Celsius.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Brandt–Daroff exercises are used as home treatment for:
questions.explanation: Repeated side-lying/sitting transitions habituate the vertigo.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Cawthorne–Cooksey exercises promote:

options.B: Vestibular compensation through gaze, head and body movements

questions.explanation: For unilateral vestibular loss.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: A positive Dix–Hallpike test shows:

options.A: Delayed, transient rotatory nystagmus with vertigo that fatigues

questions.explanation: Posterior canal BPPV.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Balance relies on integration of:
questions.explanation: Sensory Organisation Test; romberg removes vision.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: The Functional Reach Test measures:

options.C: Dynamic standing balance as the maximum distance reached forward

questions.explanation: Less than 15 cm suggests fall risk.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: The 10-metre walk test evaluates:
questions.explanation: Gait speed is considered the ‘sixth vital sign’.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: The Motor Assessment Scale (Carr & Shepherd) assesses:
questions.explanation: Eight items scored 0–6.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: In the Glasgow Coma Scale, a patient who speaks in inappropriate words scores:
questions.explanation: Verbal: 5 orientated, 4 confused, 3 inappropriate words, 2 incomprehensible sounds, 1 none.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: In the Glasgow Coma Scale, a patient who flexes abnormally (decorticate) in response to pain scores:
questions.explanation: Motor: 6 obeys, 5 localises, 4 withdraws, 3 abnormal flexion, 2 extension, 1 none.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Status epilepticus is defined as a seizure lasting longer than about:
questions.explanation: A medical emergency; first-line treatment is IV lorazepam.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Regarding exercise in people with epilepsy:

options.D: Regular exercise is beneficial, but swimming alone and unsafe heights should be avoided

questions.explanation: Supervision and seizure control determine safety.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: A child with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt who develops headache, vomiting and drowsiness may have:
questions.explanation: Urgent medical review is needed.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: A first-line drug for neuropathic pain is:
questions.explanation: NSAIDs are poor for neuropathic pain.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: Which treatment is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia?
questions.explanation: Surgical decompression is used for refractory cases.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: The commonest cause of dementia is:
questions.explanation: Memory loss and amyloid plaques, neurofibrillary tangles.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: In dementia, exercise is recommended to:

options.D: Maintain function, mobility and reduce falls

questions.explanation: Familiar, simple routines are used.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)

questions.question: The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) has a maximum score of:
questions.explanation: A score below 24 suggests cognitive impairment.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation; Shumway-Cook & Woollacott, Motor Control; standard neurology texts (chapter-level reference)
